title: Longest Valid Parentheses — stack tracking indices.
shortTitle: Longest Valid Parentheses — Stack Tracking Indices

s1_definition.profdef: The Longest Valid Parentheses problem finds the length of the longest contiguous substring of round brackets that is correctly balanced. The stack-of-indices solution pushes the index of each opening bracket and a base marker, and on each closing bracket pops and computes the length of the valid run from the current index back to the new stack top, tracking the maximum. It runs in linear time with stack space proportional to the input.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a string of grouping markers and wants the longest unbroken stretch that is perfectly balanced, ignoring any broken parts. Think of keeping a stack of positions. When you open a bracket you note its position. When you close one, you pair it off and measure how long the balanced run now extends, from here back to the last unmatched position. The widest such measured run is the answer.
s1_definition.oneliner: Push indices with a base marker, and on each close pop and measure the run back to the new top, tracking the max.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Longest Valid Parentheses problem finds the length of the longest contiguous substring of round brackets that is correctly balanced. The stack-of-indices solution pushes the index of each opening bracket and a base marker, and on each closing bracket pops and computes the length of the valid run from the current index back to the new stack top, tracking the maximum. It runs in linear time with stack space proportional to the input.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has a string of grouping markers and wants the longest unbroken stretch that is perfectly balanced, ignoring any broken parts. Think of keeping a stack of positions. When you open a bracket you note its position. When you close one, you pair it off and measure how long the balanced run now extends, from here back to the last unmatched position. The widest such measured run is the answer.

**One line to remember:** Push indices with a base marker, and on each close pop and measure the run back to the new top, tracking the max.

sections.s2_technical:
Unlike the simple validity check, here you need the length of the longest balanced run, which requires tracking positions, not just counts. The elegant method keeps a stack of indices with a sentinel base. You initialize the stack with minus one, which acts as a base marker just before the string, representing the last position that was not part of a valid substring.

You scan the string. For an opening bracket at index i, you push i onto the stack. For a closing bracket, you pop the top. Then there are two cases. If the stack is now empty, this closing bracket has no matching opener and itself becomes a new base, so you push its index as the new base marker. If the stack is not empty, the current valid run extends from just after the new top to the current index, so its length is the current index minus the new stack top, and you update the maximum with that length.

The base marker is the clever part. The value on the bottom of the stack is always the index of the most recent position that broke validity, either a minus one at the start or an unmatched closing bracket. By measuring the current index minus this base, you capture the full length of the valid substring ending at the current position, including runs that span multiple pairs like several adjacent or nested groups. This is why the stack holds indices rather than bracket characters.

A senior point is why popping before measuring is correct. When you meet a closing bracket, popping removes the matching opener's index, and the new top is the boundary of the enclosing valid run. The subtraction then spans everything from that boundary to now, which correctly includes inner completed pairs. If you measured before popping, you would miscount by one pair. Getting this order right is where subtle off-by-one bugs appear.

Another senior point is the alternative two-pass counter method, which scans left to right counting opens and closes and resets when they cross, then scans right to left symmetrically, using constant space instead of a stack. Both are linear; the stack method is the most common to explain, and I mention the two-pass counter as a constant-space variant. There is also a dynamic-programming formulation, which I note exists.

A small finance-domain example: `Deque<Integer> st=new ArrayDeque<>(); st.push(-1); int best=0; for(int i=0;i<s.length();i++){ if(s.charAt(i)=='(') st.push(i); else { st.pop(); if(st.isEmpty()) st.push(i); else best=Math.max(best, i-st.peek()); } }` finds the longest balanced run length.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India processes grouping-marker strings from partially corrupted formula fragments and wants the length of the longest contiguous balanced stretch, to recover the largest intact grouped section for salvage parsing. The fragments can be long, so the scan must be linear. Finding the longest valid parentheses run is exactly this.

This is exactly how Longest Valid Parentheses works in Java — a stack of indices with a base marker that measures each valid run back to the last unmatched position.

Problem 2 — A fragment may start with stray closing brackets or contain broken sections between valid ones, and the base marker must reset correctly at each break so runs are measured accurately, and an empty fragment gives zero. This shows the base-marker reset logic and the empty-input edge case.

What the code will do: a `LongestValidFinder` with `longestValid(String markers)` using a stack of indices with a minus-one base and pop-then-measure. The demo finds the longest balanced run in several marker strings.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the marker string `)()())`.

Step 1: the stack starts with the base marker minus one and best is zero. Index zero is `)`, a closer; we pop the minus one, the stack is now empty, so this unmatched closer becomes a new base and we push index zero. The stack is now `0`.

Step 2: index one is `(`, an opener; we push index one. The stack is `0, 1`. Index two is `)`, a closer; we pop index one, the stack top is now index zero, not empty, so the run length is the current index two minus the top zero, which is two, and best becomes two.

Step 3: index three is `(`, an opener; we push index three. The stack is `0, 3`. Index four is `)`, a closer; we pop index three, the stack top is now index zero, so the run length is index four minus zero, which is four, and best becomes four. This correctly spans the balanced run `()()` from index one through four, including both pairs.

Step 4: index five is `)`, a closer; we pop index zero, the stack becomes empty, so this unmatched closer becomes a new base and we push index five. The stack is `5`. No run is measured here because the stack was empty after popping.

Step 5: the scan ends with best four, the length of the longest balanced run `()()`. The base marker at index zero let the measurement at index four span both pairs correctly, and the resets at the stray closers kept broken sections from inflating the count. For `(()` the best is the inner `()` of length two, and an empty string gives zero.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T22:00:00Z INFO Longest valid run = 2
2026-10-26T22:00:00Z INFO Run = 2
2026-10-26T22:00:00Z INFO Longest valid run = 4
2026-10-26T22:00:00Z INFO Run = 4
2026-10-26T22:00:00Z INFO Longest valid run = 0
2026-10-26T22:00:00Z INFO Run = 0
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: ")()())"  stack=[-1] best=0
    │ scan indices; push '(' index; on ')' pop then measure or rebase
    ▼
  i0 ')' pop -1 → empty → push 0        stack=[0]
  i1 '(' push 1                         stack=[0,1]
  i2 ')' pop 1 → top 0 → len 2-0=2 best=2
  i3 '(' push 3                         stack=[0,3]
  i4 ')' pop 3 → top 0 → len 4-0=4 best=4
  i5 ')' pop 0 → empty → push 5         stack=[5]
    ▼
  best = 4  ("(()" → 2 ; "" → 0)
    ▼
  Output: longest balanced run length
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Longest Valid Finder ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Stack of INDICES with a base marker (-1 or unmatched closer) │
  │  Pop-then-measure: length = i - new stack top                 │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: finder only computes the longest valid run                │
  │  O: swap to two-pass counter (O(1) space), no caller change   │
  │  D: callers depend on the int length, not the stack           │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           LongestValidFinder          │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + longestValid(markers): int          │  O(n)/O(n)
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      longestValid contract:
        Pre:  markers non-null (else IllegalArgumentException)
        Post: length of longest balanced contiguous run
        Base marker tracks last invalid position; pop before measure

  ── State Diagram: Scan ───────────────────────────────────

  ['('] ──push i──→ [continue]
  [')'] ──pop; empty? push i (rebase) : best=max(best, i-top)──→
      │ end
      ▼
  [return best]

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. LongestValidDemo.main()
  2.   → longestValid(")()())")
  3.     → push indices, pop+measure on closers
  4.     → best grows to 4
  5.     → return 4
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Longest Valid Parentheses finds the length of the longest contiguous balanced substring of round brackets, and unlike a simple validity check it needs positions, so I use a stack of indices in linear time. I seed the stack with a minus-one base marker representing the last position that broke validity. For an opening bracket I push its index, and for a closing bracket I pop, then if the stack is empty this closer is unmatched and becomes a new base that I push, otherwise the current valid run length is the current index minus the new stack top, which I use to update the maximum.

The base marker is the heart of the method. The bottom of the stack always holds the index of the most recent position that broke validity, either the initial minus one or an unmatched closing bracket, so subtracting it from the current index captures the full length of the valid substring ending here, including runs that span several adjacent or nested pairs. That is why the stack stores indices rather than bracket characters.

The subtle correctness point is popping before measuring. When I meet a closer, popping removes the matching opener's index and the new top becomes the boundary of the enclosing valid run, so the subtraction spans every inner completed pair. Measuring before popping would miscount by one pair, which is a classic off-by-one bug here. I also know the constant-space two-pass counter variant, scanning left to right and right to left resetting when opens and closes cross, which I offer when memory is tight.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on grouping-marker strings from partially corrupted formula fragments to recover the longest intact balanced section for salvage parsing, with the base marker resetting correctly at each broken section. Explaining the index stack, the base-marker semantics, the pop-then-measure order, and the constant-space alternative shows the interviewer that I understand why this is harder than plain validity and how the index arithmetic stays correct.
